Assessment & Plan (Integrating DDx)

Key findings: Known heart failure with sub-acute increase in breathlessness on minimal exertion, new bilateral ankle edema, mild dry cough, stable vital signs on brief assessment.  
Working diagnosis: Acute decompensation of chronic (congestive) heart failure.  
Supporting evidence: prior HF diagnosis; progressive dyspnea; peripheral edema; dry cough; clinician impression; DDx model ranks HF flare as “High” likelihood.  
Management:  
• Increase Furosemide to 1 tablet twice daily (exact mg not documented).  
• Order blood tests (CBC, renal profile) to evaluate anemia, renal status prior to diuretic uptitration.  
• Arrange echocardiogram within 1–2 weeks.  
• Safety-net advice: seek care sooner for worsening dyspnea, chest pain, palpitations, dizziness.  
Considerations (lower likelihood):  
• Lower-respiratory tract infection precipitating HF (medium) – monitor for fever, sputum.  
• Pulmonary embolism (low–medium) – consider if acute deterioration or new symptoms emerge.  
• Anemia (low) – to be assessed on CBC.

Summary of Differential Diagnoses (from DDx)

1. Acute decompensated congestive heart failure – High likelihood: Established HF with new volume overload (dyspnea, bilateral ankle edema).  
2. Lower-respiratory tract infection precipitating/mimicking HF – Medium likelihood: Concurrent dry cough and malaise without objective fever; infection common HF trigger.  
3. Pulmonary embolism – Low–Medium likelihood: Sedentary occupation; acute worsening over days, but lacks pleuritic pain or unilateral swelling.
